cues.text: A Shepherd Girl of Aljustrel
Jacinta Marto was born on March 11, 1910 , in the hamlet of Aljustrel , the youngest of nine children of Manuel and Olímpia Marto.
She was affectionate almost to a fault, quick to laugh and just as quick to sulk when a game went against her.
Her family teasingly called her pouting fits "tethering the donkey."
Even as a small child she loved deeply, at five she wept on hearing the story of Christ's Passion and promised she would never make Him suffer again.
She spent her days minding sheep alongside her brother Francisco , not quite two years older, and their cousin Lúcia dos Santos, whom she adored above every other friend.
Nothing about this ordinary shepherd girl suggested she would one day be called the youngest saint in the Church's history.
Grace, as it so often does, was already working quietly in a heart most adults would have overlooked entirely.
The Angel's Visits
In 1916, a year before Our Lady herself appeared, the three cousins reported three visits from a figure who called himself the Angel of Peace.
He taught them a prayer of reparation and urged them to offer small, hidden sacrifices for sinners.
Jacinta, only six, took in this discipline as naturally as she took in everything else that moved her heart.
Something in her had already begun turning from games toward God, long before the greater visitor arrived the following May.
It was a patient, hidden preparation that every soul chosen for a great love seems to need.
A Lady Brighter Than the Sun
On May 13, 1917 , while the three were tending sheep near the Cova da Iria , a woman appeared above a small holm oak, brighter than the sun.
Jacinta, barely seven, recognized her at once as someone worth loving without holding anything back.
The Lady asked the children to pray the Rosary daily for peace and to return to that same field on the thirteenth of each month.
From that day on, Jacinta could hardly speak of anything else.
A love this immediate, this total, in a child so young, is itself one of the quiet wonders of Fátima.
The Vision That Changed Her
At the third apparition, on July 13, 1917 , the Lady opened her hands and let the children glimpse hell for a few terrible seconds.
Jacinta was marked by it more than either of the others, and heard, too, that she and Francisco would soon be called to Heaven while Lúcia remained behind.
That August a hostile local official seized the three and threatened them with death by boiling oil rather than let them recant.
Not yet eight, Jacinta simply would not say what was untrue.
By the final apparition that October, some seventy thousand people crowded a rain-soaked field and watched, as she did, the sun itself seem to dance across the sky.
A seven-year-old who has seen hell does not forget it.
Everything Jacinta did afterward, every sacrifice, every silence, traces back to those few seconds and to the Lady who showed them to her out of love, not fear.
Sacrifices of a Little Apostle
Jacinta's love was never content to stay quiet.
She asked Lúcia almost daily whether she had made any sacrifices.
She answered her own question by giving up her lunch, her games, even a visit to her sick brother, all for the conversion of sinners.
Her devotion centered, above every other object, on the Immaculate Heart of Mary; she sang of it, prayed to it, and begged that others be taught to love it as fiercely as she did.
Lúcia later recalled that in her final months Jacinta spoke, too, of wars still to come and of a Holy Father who would one day suffer greatly for the Church.
Lúcia set these words down only years afterward, once the world had begun to see them fulfilled.
It is easy to admire Jacinta's sacrifices from a comfortable distance.
It is harder to ask, as she did at seven years old, what our own comforts might be worth giving up for a soul we will never meet.
Alone, for Love of Souls
In late 1918, Jacinta fell ill with the same influenza then sweeping a war-exhausted Europe, and she never fully recovered.
Doctors moved her first to a hospital in nearby Ourém, then finally to Lisbon, hoping surgery might save her.
On February 10, 1920 , two of her ribs were removed without proper anesthetic, leaving a wound that never closed.
She bore it, by every account, without complaint, offering the pain the way she had once offered her lunch, for sinners, for the Pope, for the Immaculate Heart she loved so well.
Told she would die alone, far from her family, Jacinta accepted even that final sacrifice.
On the evening of February 20, 1920 , not yet ten years old, she asked for the sacraments and died peacefully, exactly as Our Lady had foretold.
Her last loneliness became one more gift laid at Mary's feet.
Legacy: Love Like Jacinta
Jacinta Marto was beatified alongside her brother on May 13, 2000, and canonized on May 13, 2017, the hundredth anniversary of that first apparition.
She remains the youngest saint in the Church's history who was not a martyr.
At her beatification, Pope John Paul II summed up the two children's spirituality in a phrase still repeated at Fátima today: "to contemplate like Francisco and love like Jacinta."
It fits her exactly.
Where her brother kept a silent vigil before the tabernacle, Jacinta could not stop speaking her love aloud, for Jesus, for His Mother, for every soul she feared might be lost.
We are not all asked to see what Jacinta saw or to suffer as she suffered.
But her short life keeps asking the one question she never stopped asking herself: have we made any sacrifices today, for love of the Immaculate Heart?
